links.outcome: Hallucination rate of generated diagnostic clues against source notes, Korean vs English input
links.effect: Hallucinations in 301 (30.2%) of 997 clues from Korean input vs 134 (13.4%) of 1003 clues from English-translated input.
links.quote: In contrast, clues generated from English inputs were more factually consistent, with the model producing only 134 (13.4%), falling into this category.

links.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy by input language (Korean vs English)
links.effect: Top-1 accuracy 59% (Korean) vs 74.5% (English), P<.001; top-2 accuracy comparable (90% vs 89.5%, P=.56).
links.quote: For all 200 notes, the Korean input achieved a top-1 accuracy of 59% (n=118), while the English-translated input performed better, with a top-1 accuracy of 74.5% (n=149).

links.outcome: Model performance on licensing exam questions in Korean vs English
links.effect: Exam accuracy 46.1% (53/115) in English vs 32.2% (37/115) in Korean; better in English in 7 of 11 categories.
links.quote: The model demonstrated better overall accuracy in English, answering 53 (46.1%) of 115 total questions correctly, compared to 37 (32.2%) correct answers in Korean.

links.outcome: Differential diagnosis quality and misclassification patterns by language
links.effect: With Korean input the model misclassified 24 (48%) depression and 29 (58%) anxiety cases as bipolar disorder as first impression.
links.quote: Among the 50 cases of depressive disorder, the model misclassified 24 (48%) cases as bipolar disorder as the first impression.

screen.practice: translating non-English notes to English before LLM processing
screen.reason: The study empirically tests the deployment practice of translating non-English (Korean) clinical records to English prior to prompting an open-source LLM, comparing diagnostic accuracy, relevance, and hallucination rates against native-language processing.
